title: Two guards decode the same parameter differently, and the rights object is built before the identity it is checking exists
index_line: T-0032 · CODE_EXEC · double-decoded route passthrough + a rights object defaulting to super-user · php/any-front-controller · corroborated
invariant_violated: Two assumptions in one handler. First, that two checks reading the same parameter see the same value — they do not when one decodes it a second time and the other does not. Second, that an authorization object built during bootstrap knows who the caller is — it is constructed before a public-entry-point identity is established, and an undefined role constant falls through to the most privileged branch.

mechanism.does: an unauthenticated request reaches a public participant-facing endpoint that supports a passthrough of internal files
the framework has already URL-decoded the query string once; the allowlist lookup decodes the parameter again, while the companion route restriction compares the once-decoded value
a double-encoded value resolves to the allowlisted file for one check and fails to match the string the other check compares against
the route restriction is therefore skipped and an arbitrary controller route is reachable from the public context
the front controller loads the chosen route's controller — one that was never meant to be reachable without a login
the controller's rights object was constructed before the public identity was assigned, so the unresolved role constant takes the super-user branch and the capability check passes
the import handler opens a caller-supplied stream/path argument, and the permitted wrapper is enough to reach an execution primitive
the wrapper/filter chain is escalated into code execution on the server

source.http.request.value: the public endpoint's parameters: the passthrough selector, the route, and the import stream — three fields that only matter together

sink.file.read.value: the framework's file/stream open, reached with a caller-chosen wrapper or path

guard.resolve-check.value: the allowlist-plus-route-restriction pair: two checks, two decodings, one value

encoding.path.value: double-encoded forms (`%2569ndex.php`) chosen so the two decodings disagree

oracle.error.value: the framework's error surface tells you which of the two checks you satisfied — use it to tune the encoding

preconditions.expr: a public (unauthenticated) entry point exists that passes through to internal files or controllers
one guard decodes the parameter a second time while the other does not
the rights/authorization object is instantiated before the public identity is established, and an undefined role constant is treated as privileged
version is in the affected range

success: a double-encoded passthrough value is accepted while the plain one is rejected (or vice versa) — that asymmetry is the bug
an internal controller's output or error appears in a response to an unauthenticated request
the stream parameter's error names a wrapper or filter rather than a missing file, showing the read happened
failure_like: both checks operate on the same decoded value — one encoding, one answer
the rights object is built only after the public identity is set, or an undefined role resolves to the least-privileged branch
false_positive: a 200 from the public endpoint that never leaves the allowlist — confirm the response body came from the internal controller
an error page mentioning the controller name because the route was rejected, not executed
claiming the shell from the encoding trick alone: the route reachability and the rights-order defect are separate links in the chain

hazards: audit decode counts: any parameter that two checks read must be decoded the same number of times. Grep every `urldecode($_GET...)` — it is almost always the bug
bootstrap ordering is the second half: a rights object created before the identity exists is a default-allow bug, and undefined-constant fall-through makes it privileged
the reachable controller is chosen at runtime, so enumerate the route map and pick the one whose parameters are most dangerous
public-facing entry points (surveys, forms, previews, password resets) deliberately define NOAUTH and then build privilege state — read those handlers first
non_transfers: frameworks that decode once, into a single normalised request object that every guard shares
rights objects constructed lazily after the identity is resolved
controller dispatch that re-applies the route's own access policy after passthrough

evidence.target: Vanderbilt REDCap survey passthrough + Data Import (CVE-2026-90817)
